name: Caoineag
description: A female death-portent spirit of the Scottish Highlands, associated particularly with certain clans, who weeps at waterfalls, streams, and lonely places before a death — most famously before the Massacre of Glencoe.
full_description: The Caoineag (Scottish Gaelic for 'the weeper') is a female spirit of the Scottish Highlands whose lamentation is heard before deaths, especially violent or mass deaths. She is normally invisible and is heard wailing at waterfalls, in glens, by streams, and on mountainsides. Unlike the related bean nighe (the 'washer at the ford'), the Caoineag cannot be approached, questioned, or compelled to grant wishes. She is closely associated with specific clans, including Clan MacDonald of Glencoe, whose Caoineag was said to wail repeatedly the night before the 1692 Massacre of Glencoe. The closely related Caointeach is recorded in Islay tradition as a green-shawled figure heard outside the homes of those about to die. The figure is documented in Alexander Carmichael's Carmina Gadelica and in Edward Dwelly's Scottish Gaelic dictionary, and is part of a broader Gaelic family of female death-portent beings that includes the Irish bean sídhe (banshee).

aliases.name: Caointeach
aliases.meaning: regional variant; appears outside the homes of the soon-to-die wearing a green shawl

origin: Scottish Highlands and the Hebrides, with strong attestation in Lochaber (Glencoe), Argyll, and Islay.

etymology.origin: Scottish Gaelic caoin- ('to weep, lament') with the feminine agent suffix -eag.
etymology.first_use: Recorded in Scottish Gaelic oral tradition; published English-language records in the 19th and early 20th centuries (Carmichael, Campbell, Dwelly).

timeline.event: Massacre of Glencoe; later Highland tradition holds that the Caoineag of Clan MacDonald wailed nightly before the killings
timeline.significance: The most-cited single legend involving the Caoineag
timeline.source: Highland oral tradition; recorded in Carmichael (1900) and later sources

timeline.event: Alexander Carmichael publishes Carmina Gadelica, including material on the Caoineag
timeline.significance: First major scholarly publication of the tradition in English
timeline.source: Carmichael, A., Carmina Gadelica vol. II

timeline.event: Edward Dwelly's Illustrated Gaelic-English Dictionary appears, defining caoineag among Scottish Gaelic supernatural terms
timeline.significance: Lexical attestation in the standard Gaelic dictionary

related.name: Bean sídhe (Banshee)
related.description: Irish female death-portent spirit; the closest cognate to the Caoineag

related.name: Bean nighe
related.description: Scottish Gaelic 'washer at the ford' — a related, but distinct, death-portent figure who can be approached

related.name: Caointeach
related.description: Islay variant of the Caoineag, appearing in a green shawl

cultural_notes: In Highland Gaelic tradition, the Caoineag is understood as a real spirit-being whose lamentation warns of impending death. She is feared and respected rather than venerated.
